tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Inventory API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /inventory/{skuId}:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: CW-XYCS-BM-01
    get:
      summary: Get inventory for a SKU
      description: Returns the current quantity on hand for the specified SKU. Returns 404 if the SKU does not exist.
      operationId: getInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current inventory state for the sku
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
    post:
      summary: Create or update inventory for a SKU
      description: >
        Adds stock for the specified SKU. If the SKU does not yet exist in inventory,
        it is created with the given quantity. If it already exists, the quantity is
        added to the current stock. Returns the updated inventory state for the SKU.
      operationId: createInventory
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current state of the item after update
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory/{skuId}/purchase:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: widget
    post:
      summary: Purchase a quantity of a SKU
      description: >
        Deducts the requested quantity from inventory for the specified SKU.
        The purchase is only allowed if the current stock is sufficient to
        fulfill the full requested quantity. Returns 404 if the SKU does not
        exist. Returns 400 if there is insufficient inventory. On success, returns the
        remaining inventory for the SKU.
      operationId: purchaseItem
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Purchase successful; remaining inventory for the item
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Insufficient inventory or invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory:
    get:
      summary: List all inventory
      description: >
        Returns a list of all SKUs currently in inventory along with their quantities.
        If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array.
      operationId: listInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of all inventory items
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'  
components:
  schemas:
    InventoryQuantity:
      type: object
      required:
        - quantity
      properties:
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          example: 10
    InventoryItem:
      type: object
      properties:
        skuId:
          type: string
          example: widget
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          example: 10
    Error:
      type: string
      example: Insufficient inventory

11	## Endpoints

13	| Method | Path | Behavior | Responses | Status |

15	| `GET` | `/inventory` | List every SKU and its quantity (`[]` when empty) | `200` JSON array | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |
16	| `GET` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Current quantity for one SKU (`404` body: `SKU not found: <skuId>`) | `200` JSON, `404` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |
17	| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Add stock; creates the SKU if it is new (one atomic upsert) | `200` JSON, `400` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed; walkthrough pending |
18	| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}/purchase` | Deduct stock, only if enough is on hand | `200` JSON, `400` / `404` text | Not started |

20	Request bodies are `{"quantity": <integer ≥ 1>}`. Success bodies are
21	`{"skuId": "...", "quantity": <integer ≥ 0>}`. Error bodies are plain-text strings

24	## Tech stack
25	
26	| Choice | Why |
27	| --- | --- |
28	| **Kotlin** (JVM) | Nuuly's production language, and one I want to learn in depth (see [Learning Kotlin](#learning-kotlin-with-this-project)). |
29	| **Spring Boot**, Spring MVC | Nuuly's production framework. Nuuly evaluated Micronaut and found its speed gains didn't outweigh the environment problems it caused, so they chose Spring (see below). |
30	| **Gradle, Kotlin DSL** | The standard build for Kotlin and Spring. Build scripts are written in Kotlin too. |
31	| **PostgreSQL 18** + **Flyway** | The database enforces the no-oversell rule; Flyway applies versioned SQL migrations at startup. See the decision record below. |
32	| **JUnit 6** (Jupiter) + Spring test support | Controller tests via `MockMvc`, plus full-context integration tests. |
33	| **Testcontainers** | Tests run against a real Postgres in Docker, never an in-memory stand-in. |
34	
35	Pinned versions: **Spring Boot 4.1.1**, **Kotlin 2.3.21**, **Java 21** (Gradle toolchain),
36	**Gradle 9.7.1** (wrapper), **PostgreSQL 18**. The project was generated with Spring
37	Initializr and then trimmed by hand; the exact command is in the commit
38	"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr".
39	
40	**Why Spring rather than Micronaut.** Seth, an architect at Nuuly, told me the team moved to

77	RETURNING sku_id, quantity;

97	JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.

100	control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in

## 1. The contract

```yaml
/inventory/{skuId}/purchase:
  post:
    description: >
      Deducts the requested quantity from inventory for the specified SKU.
      The purchase is only allowed if the current stock is sufficient to
      fulfill the full requested quantity. Returns 404 if the SKU does not
      exist. Returns 400 if there is insufficient inventory. On success, returns the
      remaining inventory for the SKU.
    requestBody: required, application/json, InventoryQuantity   # quantity: integer, minimum 1
    responses:
      '200': application/json InventoryItem   # remaining stock
      '400': text/plain Error                 # "Insufficient inventory or invalid request"; example: "Insufficient inventory"
      '404': text/plain Error                 # SKU not found
```

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase` with `{"quantity": n}` and enough stock returns `200` JSON `{"skuId", "quantity": <remaining>}`
- [ ] Buying exactly the stock on hand leaves quantity `0`, and the row stays, so `GET` still shows it
- [ ] Buying more than is on hand returns `400` `text/plain`, and stock is unchanged (no partial fill)
- [ ] An unknown SKU returns `404` `text/plain` `SKU not found: <skuId>`
- [ ] Invalid requests return `400` `text/plain` with the same rules as `POST /inventory/{skuId}` (`quantity < 1`, malformed/strict JSON, wrong Content-Type). Your existing `@RestControllerAdvice` handlers should cover these for free, and the tests will prove it.
- [ ] Never oversells under concurrency: N > S concurrent purchases → exactly S succeed, final quantity is 0, never negative

**Things I'm settling by convention** (tell me if you disagree):
- If a request is both invalid and for an unknown SKU (e.g. `quantity: 0` on a missing SKU), it gets **400**. Spring validates the body before your code runs, and this matches how POST already behaves.
- SKU matching stays exact and case-sensitive, as decided for POST.

Two decisions are yours:

questions.question: The atomic UPDATE ... WHERE sku_id = ? AND quantity >= ? returns no row in two cases: the SKU is missing (404) or the stock is too low (400). How should we tell them apart?

options.label: UPDATE, then look up (Recommended)
options.description: Repository gets removeStock(skuId, qty): InventoryItem? (the atomic UPDATE). If it returns null, the service calls the existing findBySkuId: null → SkuNotFoundException (404), otherwise InsufficientInventoryException (400). The decision to sell stays atomic, so there is no oversell risk. The only race is cosmetic: if a SKU is created between the two statements, you get 400 instead of 404.

options.label: One SQL statement (CTE)
options.description: A single query with a CTE that does the UPDATE and also reports whether the row exists. Fully atomic classification, but the SQL is harder to read and explain in the interview.

options.description: A @Transactional read with a row lock, check in Kotlin, then write. It works, but it's the locking approach the README decision record rejected in favor of single statements.

## 2. Plan

**Your decisions:** one CTE statement for the purchase, and the 400 body is `Insufficient inventory for <skuId>`.

That one statement has **three** outcomes: purchased, SKU missing, or not enough stock. A nullable return (`InventoryItem?`, like `addStock`) can only express two, so the repository needs a return type that can hold three. In Kotlin that's a **sealed interface**.

### Files you'll write (request-path order)

| # | File | Layer | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `inventory/PurchaseResult.kt` (new) | model | `sealed interface PurchaseResult` with three cases: `Purchased(val item: InventoryItem)` (a data class), `SkuNotFound` and `InsufficientStock` (both `data object`s) |
| 2 | `InventoryRepository.removeStock(skuId: String, quantity: Int): PurchaseResult` | repository | One SQL statement. A `WITH` CTE runs the conditional `UPDATE … WHERE sku_id = :skuId AND quantity >= :quantity RETURNING …`, and the outer `SELECT` returns one row with the remaining quantity (NULL if nothing was updated) plus whether the SKU exists. You then map that row to one of the three cases. |
| 3 | `error/InsufficientInventoryException(skuId: String)` (new) | error | `RuntimeException` with the message `Insufficient inventory for <skuId>`. It follows the same pattern as `SkuNotFoundException`. |
| 4 | `InventoryService.purchaseInventory(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem` | service | `require(quantity >= 1)` as in `receiveInventory`, then a `when` over the `PurchaseResult`: `Purchased` → return the item, `SkuNotFound` → throw `SkuNotFoundException`, `InsufficientStock` → throw `InsufficientInventoryException` |
| 5 | `InventoryController.purchaseInventory` | controller | `@PostMapping("/{skuId}/purchase")`, `@PathVariable` + `@Valid @RequestBody InventoryQuantity`, delegates to the service |
| 6 | `InventoryExceptionHandler.handleInsufficientInventory` | error | Maps `InsufficientInventoryException` to a 400 `text/plain` response. Also update the `// Contract:` comments on the existing handlers, since they now serve the purchase endpoint too. |

The names mirror what you already have: `addStock`/`removeStock` in the repository and `receiveInventory`/`purchaseInventory` in the service. Rename anything you like before I write the tests.

### Tests I'll write

| File | New tests | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `InventoryRepositoryTest` | ~7 | Partial purchase → `Purchased(remaining)`; exact stock → `Purchased(0)` with the row still there; stock + 1 → `InsufficientStock`, unchanged; zero stock → `InsufficientStock`; missing → `SkuNotFound` and no row created; case-sensitive; a decoy row is untouched |
| `InventoryServiceTest` | ~4 | Maps each outcome to its item or exception; `quantity < 1` → `IllegalArgumentException`, stock unchanged |
| `InventoryControllerTest` | ~8 | 200 JSON with the remaining stock; exact → 0; 400 `Insufficient inventory for widget`; 404 `SKU not found: missing`; `quantity < 1`, unreadable body and wrong Content-Type all → 400 (proving your existing handlers cover the new route); invalid body on a missing SKU → 400, not 404; case-sensitive |
| `InventoryConcurrencyTest` | 3 × `@RepeatedTest(5)` | From the oversell plan: **same-SKU race** (stock 10, 50 buyers of 1 → exactly 10 succeed, final 0), **uneven quantities** (sum of successful purchases ≤ stock, final = stock − sum), **mixed receive + purchase** (final = initial + received − purchased) |

The negative control, multi-instance test and load test stay on the TODO for later.

### New concepts (your coaching list and the walkthrough agenda)

- **Kotlin:** `sealed interface`, `data object`, `when` as an exhaustive expression with no `else`, `is` checks and smart casts inside `when` branches
- **SQL:** data-modifying CTEs (`WITH x AS (UPDATE … RETURNING …) SELECT …`), scalar subqueries and `EXISTS`, and why every part of one statement sees the same snapshot (interview material)
- **JDBC:** SQL `NULL` vs `rs.getInt`. There's a trap here that the tests will catch. I'll let you find it.

Approve this plan, or tell me what to change, and I'll write the failing tests.

39	  see it. Worse, each worker's upsert would wait on that row's lock, which the test thread holds

54	
55	```kotlin
56	// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
57	// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
58	private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
59	    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
60	    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
61	    val start = CountDownLatch(1)

63	        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
64	            pool.submit(Callable {
65	                ready.countDown()
66	                start.await()
67	                action(i)
68	            })
69	        }
70	        ready.await()
71	        start.countDown()

73	    } finally {
74	        pool.shutdownNow()
75	    }
76	}
77	```

80	first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
81	makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.

83	**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements

85

87	   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.

89	   `start.countDown()` releases all of them at once.

92	thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:
93	the queued tasks could never arrive at `ready`). `submit` returns a `Future`; `get(30, SECONDS)`

96	stops the threads even when something failed.

103	`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
104	`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.

106	**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
107	(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
108	conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).
109	
110	**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
111	`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.
112	
113	**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a
114	`Result`: a success holding the value, or a failure holding the exception. Nothing is thrown.
115	That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.
116	`exceptionOrNull()` and `getOrNull()` read the two sides. Java has no built-in equivalent; you'd
117	catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.

119	### The new-SKU creation race
120	
121	```kotlin
122	@RepeatedTest(5)
123	fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
124	    val threads = 50
125	
126	    val results = race(threads) { i -> inventoryRepository.addStock("new-sku", i + 1) }
127	
128	    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
129	    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
130	    assertTrue(results.all { it.getOrNull() != null }, "an add returned null (treated as overflow)")
131	    assertEquals((1..threads).sum(), quantityOf("new-sku"))
132	}

136	row exists, then either `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. Two threads can both see "no row" and both
137	`INSERT`. The second one fails with a duplicate-key error (the primary key), and its stock is
138	lost. A single `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement can't split like that: Postgres
139	handles the conflict inside the one statement.

142	losing one add and double-counting another would cancel out. With 1, 2, ..., 50 the expected

144

146	leaving only the exceptions. `all { }` is `true` if the condition holds for every element.
147	`(1..threads).sum()` adds up an inclusive range (`..` includes the end, `until` doesn't).
148	
149	**Kotlin: assertion messages.** The last argument of `assertTrue` is the message printed on
150	failure. `"adds failed: $failures"` shows *which* exceptions happened, which beats a bare
151	"expected true".
152	
153	**JUnit: `@RepeatedTest(5)`.** Runs the test five times, each a separate result with its own
154	`@BeforeEach`. Races are intermittent; a broken implementation might pass once by luck, but
155	rarely five times in a row.

158	
159	```kotlin
160	@RepeatedTest(5)
161	fun `concurrent adds to an existing SKU are never lost`() {
162	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', 10)").update()

174	threads that both read 10 both write 12, and one add disappears. That's a *lost update*. With

### Why a full context and not `@JdbcTest`

```kotlin

// only: rows it inserts stay invisible to the worker threads, and the workers' commits escape the rollback.
/**
 * Oversell test plan, concurrency section: ...
```

thread and rolls it back at the end. Spring ties that transaction to the **thread**. Worker

commits on its own. That causes two problems:

- A row the test inserts before the race (`widget` with 10) is uncommitted, so the workers can't
  see it. Worse, each worker's upsert would wait on that row's lock, which the test thread holds
  until the rollback, so the race would hang until the timeout.
- The workers' rows are committed for real, so the rollback wouldn't clean them up, and they'd
  leak into the next test.

and the `@BeforeEach` `DELETE` does the cleanup (the same pattern as
[InventoryControllerTest.kt](InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)).

```kotlin
// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
    try {
        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
            pool.submit(Callable {
                ready.countDown()
                start.await()
                action(i)
            })
        }
        ready.await()
        start.countDown()
        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
    } finally {
        pool.shutdownNow()
    }
}
```

**Why a gate at all:** starting 50 threads one by one in a loop spreads them out in time. The
first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.

**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements
it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. There are two latches here:

1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single

thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:

stops the threads even when something failed.

**Kotlin: a generic function.** `fun <T> race(..., action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>>` works for
any result type. `T` is whatever `action` returns: `InventoryItem?` for `addStock`, and later
something else for purchases. Java writes it the same way: `<T> List<Result<T>> race(...)`.

**Kotlin: function types.** `action: (Int) -> T` is a parameter that holds a function taking an
`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.

**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).

**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.

**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a

That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.

catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.

### The new-SKU creation race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i -> inventoryRepository.addStock("new-sku", i + 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
```

row exists, then either `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. Two threads can both see "no row" and both

lost. A single `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement can't split like that: Postgres

**Why each thread adds a different amount (`i + 1`):** if every thread added the same amount,
losing one add and double-counting another would cancel out. With 1, 2, ..., 50 the expected
total is `(1..50).sum()` = 1275, and a lost or repeated add shows up in the final number.

**Kotlin: `mapNotNull`, `all`, `sum`.** `mapNotNull` maps each element and drops the `null`s,

**Kotlin: assertion messages.** The last argument of `assertTrue` is the message printed on
failure. `"adds failed: $failures"` shows *which* exceptions happened, which beats a bare

**JUnit: `@RepeatedTest(5)`.** Runs the test five times, each a separate result with its own
`@BeforeEach`. Races are intermittent; a broken implementation might pass once by luck, but
rarely five times in a row.

### The lost-update race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent adds to an existing SKU are never lost`() {
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', 10)").update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 2) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")

```

**What it catches:** a read-then-write implementation (read 10, compute 12, write 12). Two
threads that both read 10 both write 12, and one add disappears. That's a *lost update*. With
`SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity`, Postgres does the read and the write
under a row lock inside one statement, so the second thread waits and then adds to 12.

**Kotlin: an implicit lambda parameter.** `race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock(...) }`
doesn't use the index, so the lambda declares no parameter. A lambda with one parameter can
leave it out; if needed, it's available as `it`.

## Check your understanding

- Why would these tests be unreliable under `@JdbcTest`? Give both reasons.
- What happens to the race if you delete the `start` latch and keep only `ready`? And if you
  delete both?
- Why must the thread pool have `threads` threads, and not, say, 10?
- The new-SKU test adds `i + 1` rather than a constant. Describe a bug the constant version
  would miss.
- `race` returns `List<Result<T>>` instead of throwing on the first failure. What would the
  test report lose if it threw?
- Why run each test five times? Does passing five times prove there's no race?

35	
36	```kotlin
37	/**
38	 * [InventoryService] preconditions that hold even when the controller's `@Valid` check is bypassed
39	 * (a direct Kotlin caller). Runs against a real Postgres; each test is rolled back.
40	 */
41	@JdbcTest
42	@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class, InventoryRepository::class, InventoryService::class)
43	class InventoryServiceTest @Autowired constructor(
44	    private val inventoryService: InventoryService,
45	    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
46	) {

50	[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md#a-jdbc-test-slice)): real Postgres, no
51	web layer, no component scan, every test rolled back. Because component scanning is off,
52	`InventoryService` has to be listed in `@Import` too, next to the repository it depends on. Spring
53	then builds the service with the repository injected, exactly as in the running app.
54	`@Autowired constructor` is needed because JUnit, not Spring, creates the test class (see
55	[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).
56

58	called, but only the real table shows that the stored stock is unchanged, whatever path the code
59	took. It also showed what really happened *before* the fix (the table below), which a mock would
60	have hidden.

63	
64	```kotlin
65	private fun insert(skuId: String, quantity: Int) {
66	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)")
67	        .params(skuId, quantity)
68	        .update()
69	}

71	private fun quantityOf(skuId: String): Int? =
72	    jdbcClient.sql("SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = ?")
73	        .param(skuId)
74	        .query { rs, _ -> rs.getInt("quantity") }
75	        .list()
76	        .singleOrNull()
77	```

80	there, including the positional `?` placeholders filled by `.params(...)`. They set up and read rows
81	with plain SQL, so the test doesn't use the code under test to check itself.

84	
85	```kotlin
86	// Why: a programming error, not a client error, so IllegalArgumentException (a 500), not a 400.
87	/** A quantity below 1 is refused before the database is touched, and an existing SKU is unchanged. */
88	@ParameterizedTest(name = "quantity {0}")
89	@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])
90	fun `receiveInventory rejects a quantity below 1 for an existing SKU`(quantity: Int) {
91	    insert("widget", 5)

100	`@ValueSource` runs the method once per value (see
101	[InventoryControllerTest.kt](InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)).

104	three layers, each for a different audience:
105	
106	| Layer | Catches | Result |
107	| --- | --- | --- |
108	| `@Valid` + `@Min` (controller) | a bad client request | 400 with a message |
109	| `require` (service) | a bad call from our own code | 500: we have a bug |
110	| `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` (database) | anything that got past both | 500 |
111	
112	So there is deliberately no handler mapping `IllegalArgumentException` to 400.
113	
114	**Why both 0 and -5:** they failed in different ways before `require` existed. `0` *succeeded*:

116	`CHECK` allows 0. `-5` failed with a Postgres error (the overflow guard's `MAX - (-5)` for an

118	`DataIntegrityViolationException`, far from the real cause.
119

122	```kotlin

124	@ParameterizedTest(name = "quantity {0}")
125	@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])
126	fun `receiveInventory rejects a quantity below 1 for a new SKU`(quantity: Int) {
127	    assertFailsWith<IllegalArgumentException> { inventoryService.receiveInventory("new-sku", quantity) }
128	    assertNull(quantityOf("new-sku"))
129	}
130	```
131	
132	`assertNull` proves the row doesn't exist, which catches the phantom zero-stock SKU that `0`
133	used to create.
134

137	1. The controller already rejects `quantity: 0` with a 400. Why can the service still receive a 0?
138	2. Before `require` was added, what did `receiveInventory("new-sku", 0)` do, and why didn't the
139	   database stop it?

```kotlin
private fun insert(skuId: String, quantity: Int) {
```

### The same-SKU purchase race

```kotlin
// Why: the "remaining" values prove each unit was sold exactly once. Two buyers who both read
// stock 10 and wrote 9 would both see 9, and 0..9 would not come back as a clean set.
/**
 * Same-SKU purchase race: with stock S and N > S buyers of 1, exactly S succeed, N - S are refused
 * as insufficient stock, and the SKU ends at 0, never negative.
 */
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases never sell more than the stock`() {
    val stock = 10
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
    assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining)
    assertEquals(threads - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock })
    assertEquals(0, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** the oversell itself. The naive purchase reads the stock, checks
`stock >= quantity` in Kotlin, then writes `stock - quantity`. Between the read and the write,
another buyer can do the same, and both sell the same last unit. The conditional
`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :quantity` does the check and the write in one statement under a row
lock, so the second buyer waits and then re-checks against the new value.

**Three assertions, three kinds of bug:**

1. `remaining == [0, 1, ..., 9]`: each successful buyer saw a *different* remaining quantity, so
   each of the 10 units was sold exactly once. A lost update would show a repeated value.
2. Exactly `threads - stock` (40) were refused as `InsufficientStock`, and none were reported as
   `SkuNotFound`, which would be the wrong error for a SKU that exists.
3. The final quantity is 0: not negative (oversold) and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock
   remained).

**Kotlin: `getOrThrow()`.** Reads a `Result`'s value, or rethrows its exception. It's safe here
because the line before already asserted there are no failures.

**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.

**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock` works because a
`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`. `count { ... }` counts the elements
that match.

### Uneven quantities

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases of different sizes never oversell`() {
    val stock = 100
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        val quantity = i % 7 + 1
        quantity to inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", quantity)
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    assertTrue(outcomes.none { (_, result) -> result == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound }, "an existing SKU was reported missing")
    val sold = outcomes.filter { (_, result) -> result is PurchaseResult.Purchased }.sumOf { (quantity, _) -> quantity }
    assertTrue(sold <= stock, "sold $sold of $stock")
    assertEquals(stock - sold, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

`> 0` instead of `>= :quantity`. The buyers ask for 1 to 7 units (`i % 7 + 1`), about 200 in total
against a stock of 100, so the SKU runs low and a big order can be refused while a small one
still fits.

**Why not assert an exact count:** which buyers win depends on thread timing, so the test asserts
the invariant instead. What was sold never exceeds the stock, and the database agrees exactly with
what the successful buyers were told.

**Kotlin: `to` and `Pair`.** `quantity to result` builds a `Pair(quantity, result)`. `to` is an
*infix* function: called without a dot or parentheses. Each thread returns what it asked for next
to what happened, so the test can add up the successful quantities.

**Kotlin: destructuring in lambdas.** `{ (_, result) -> ... }` unpacks the `Pair` into its two
parts right in the parameter list; `_` skips the part the lambda doesn't need. `sumOf { }` adds up
whatever the lambda returns for each element.

### Restocks mixed with purchases

```kotlin
// Why: demand (30 x 5 = 150) exceeds supply (20 + 30 x 3 = 110), so some purchases are refused
// and the test exercises both outcomes under contention.
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent restocks and purchases keep an exact balance`() {
    val initial = 20
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(initial).update()
    val threads = 60

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        if (i % 2 == 0) {
            checkNotNull(inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 3)) { "restock refused" }
            3
        } else {
            when (inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 5)) {
                is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> -5
                PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> 0
                PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> error("an existing SKU was reported missing")
            }
        }
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "operations failed: $failures")
    assertEquals(initial + results.sumOf { it.getOrThrow() }, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** interference between the two writes. The upsert and the conditional
`UPDATE` both lock the same row; if either did a read-then-write, a restock could overwrite a
purchase (or the other way round) and the books wouldn't balance. Each thread returns its change
to the stock (`+3`, `-5` or `0`), and the final quantity must equal the initial one plus the sum
of the changes.

**Kotlin: `if` and `when` are expressions.** The lambda's last expression is its return value, and
here that's an `if`/`else` whose branches end in `3` or a `when`. In Java both would be
statements, and you'd need a variable or `return`s.

**Kotlin: an exhaustive `when` over a sealed type.** `PurchaseResult` is sealed, so the compiler
knows all its cases. This `when` lists all three and needs no `else`. If someone adds a fourth
case, this code stops compiling until it's handled. `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` checks the type
(a data class, with a new instance each time), while the two objects are compared by value.

**Kotlin: `checkNotNull` and `error`.** `checkNotNull(x) { "msg" }` returns `x` if it isn't null,
otherwise throws `IllegalStateException("msg")`. `error("msg")` always throws one. Inside `race`,
`runCatching` collects that exception, so the `failures` assertion reports it.

# InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-29

## Role

This is the first part of the **concurrency** section of the oversell test plan in
[TODO.md](../../../../../.claude/TODO.md). Many threads call `InventoryRepository.addStock` for the
same SKU at the same moment, and the tests check that no update is lost and none fails. The
purchase race tests will join this class when `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase` exists.

The other test classes send one request at a time, so they can't catch a race. This one can.

## Walkthrough

### Why a full context and not `@JdbcTest`

```kotlin
// Why: @SpringBootTest, not @JdbcTest. @JdbcTest's rolled-back transaction belongs to the test thread
// only: rows it inserts stay invisible to the worker threads, and the workers' commits escape the rollback.
/**
 * Oversell test plan, concurrency section: ...
 */
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryConcurrencyTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val inventoryRepository: InventoryRepository,
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {
```

**Spring: test transactions are per thread.** `@JdbcTest` (see
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)) opens a transaction on the test's
thread and rolls it back at the end. Spring ties that transaction to the **thread**. Worker
threads started by the test aren't part of it: each takes its own connection from the pool and
commits on its own. That causes two problems:

- A row the test inserts before the race (`widget` with 10) is uncommitted, so the workers can't
  see it. Worse, each worker's upsert would wait on that row's lock, which the test thread holds
  until the rollback, so the race would hang until the timeout.
- The workers' rows are committed for real, so the rollback wouldn't clean them up, and they'd
  leak into the next test.

So this class runs with no test transaction. Every call commits, exactly like in production,
and the `@BeforeEach` `DELETE` does the cleanup (the same pattern as
[InventoryControllerTest.kt](InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)).

**Spring: context caching.** These annotations differ from `InventoryControllerTest` (there's no
`@AutoConfigureMockMvc`), so Spring caches a separate context for this class, with its own
Postgres container. That costs a few seconds of startup, and in return the class doesn't depend on
MockMvc, which isn't meant to be called from many threads.

### The start gate

```kotlin
// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
    try {
        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
            pool.submit(Callable {
                ready.countDown()
                start.await()
                action(i)
            })
        }
        ready.await()
        start.countDown()
        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
    } finally {
        pool.shutdownNow()
    }
}
```

**Why a gate at all:** starting 50 threads one by one in a loop spreads them out in time. The
first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.

**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements
it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. There are two latches here:

1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single

### The same-SKU purchase race

```kotlin
// Why: the "remaining" values prove each unit was sold exactly once. Two buyers who both read
// stock 10 and wrote 9 would both see 9, and 0..9 would not come back as a clean set.
/**
 * Same-SKU purchase race: with stock S and N > S buyers of 1, exactly S succeed, N - S are refused
 * as insufficient stock, and the SKU ends at 0, never negative.
 */
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases never sell more than the stock`() {
    val stock = 10
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
    assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining)
    assertEquals(threads - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock })
    assertEquals(0, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** the oversell itself. The naive purchase reads the stock, checks
`stock >= quantity` in Kotlin, then writes `stock - quantity`. Between the read and the write,
another buyer can do the same, and both sell the same last unit. The conditional
`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :quantity` does the check and the write in one statement under a row
lock, so the second buyer waits and then re-checks against the new value.

**Three assertions, three kinds of bug:**

1. `remaining == [0, 1, ..., 9]`: each successful buyer saw a *different* remaining quantity, so
   each of the 10 units was sold exactly once. A lost update would show a repeated value.
2. Exactly `threads - stock` (40) were refused as `InsufficientStock`, and none were reported as
   `SkuNotFound`, which would be the wrong error for a SKU that exists.
3. The final quantity is 0: not negative (oversold) and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock
   remained).

**Kotlin: `getOrThrow()`.** Reads a `Result`'s value, or rethrows its exception. It's safe here
because the line before already asserted there are no failures.

**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.

**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock` works because a
`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`. `count { ... }` counts the elements
that match.

### Uneven quantities

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases of different sizes never oversell`() {
    val stock = 100
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        val quantity = i % 7 + 1
        quantity to inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", quantity)
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    assertTrue(outcomes.none { (_, result) -> result == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound }, "an existing SKU was reported missing")
    val sold = outcomes.filter { (_, result) -> result is PurchaseResult.Purchased }.sumOf { (quantity, _) -> quantity }
    assertTrue(sold <= stock, "sold $sold of $stock")
    assertEquals(stock - sold, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** a check that only works for purchases of 1, for example comparing against
`> 0` instead of `>= :quantity`. The buyers ask for 1 to 7 units (`i % 7 + 1`), about 200 in total
against a stock of 100, so the SKU runs low and a big order can be refused while a small one
still fits.

**Why not assert an exact count:** which buyers win depends on thread timing, so the test asserts
the invariant instead. What was sold never exceeds the stock, and the database agrees exactly with
what the successful buyers were told.

**Kotlin: `to` and `Pair`.** `quantity to result` builds a `Pair(quantity, result)`. `to` is an
*infix* function: called without a dot or parentheses. Each thread returns what it asked for next
to what happened, so the test can add up the successful quantities.

**Kotlin: destructuring in lambdas.** `{ (_, result) -> ... }` unpacks the `Pair` into its two
parts right in the parameter list; `_` skips the part the lambda doesn't need. `sumOf { }` adds up
whatever the lambda returns for each element.

### Restocks mixed with purchases

```kotlin
// Why: demand (30 x 5 = 150) exceeds supply (20 + 30 x 3 = 110), so some purchases are refused
// and the test exercises both outcomes under contention.
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent restocks and purchases keep an exact balance`() {
    val initial = 20
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(initial).update()
    val threads = 60

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        if (i % 2 == 0) {
            checkNotNull(inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 3)) { "restock refused" }
            3
        } else {
            when (inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 5)) {
                is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> -5
                PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> 0
                PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> error("an existing SKU was reported missing")
            }
        }
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "operations failed: $failures")
    assertEquals(initial + results.sumOf { it.getOrThrow() }, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** interference between the two writes. The upsert and the conditional
`UPDATE` both lock the same row; if either did a read-then-write, a restock could overwrite a
purchase (or the other way round) and the books wouldn't balance. Each thread returns its change
to the stock (`+3`, `-5` or `0`), and the final quantity must equal the initial one plus the sum
of the changes.

**Kotlin: `if` and `when` are expressions.** The lambda's last expression is its return value, and
here that's an `if`/`else` whose branches end in `3` or a `when`. In Java both would be
statements, and you'd need a variable or `return`s.

**Kotlin: an exhaustive `when` over a sealed type.** `PurchaseResult` is sealed, so the compiler
knows all its cases. This `when` lists all three and needs no `else`. If someone adds a fourth
case, this code stops compiling until it's handled. `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` checks the type
(a data class, with a new instance each time), while the two objects are compared by value.

**Kotlin: `checkNotNull` and `error`.** `checkNotNull(x) { "msg" }` returns `x` if it isn't null,
otherwise throws `IllegalStateException("msg")`. `error("msg")` always throws one. Inside `race`,
`runCatching` collects that exception, so the `failures` assertion reports it.

# InventoryControllerTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-29

## Role

Tests `GET /inventory`, `GET /inventory/{skuId}` and `POST /inventory/{skuId}` through the whole
stack: MockMvc → controller → service → repository → real Postgres. It checks exactly what the
contract specifies: the status code, the `Content-Type` and the exact body (JSON on success, plain
text on `400`/`404`). For `POST` it also reads the table afterwards, so a rejected request is
proven to have changed nothing.

## Walkthrough

### Full context plus MockMvc

```kotlin
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryControllerTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val mockMvc: MockMvc,
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {
```

**Spring: `@SpringBootTest` + `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`.** `@SpringBootTest` starts the full
application context (see [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](../InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md)).
`@AutoConfigureMockMvc` adds a `MockMvc` bean. `MockMvc` sends a fake HTTP request straight into
Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet`, in the same JVM and on the same thread, with no real server or
network port. Everything after that is real: request mapping, the controller, Jackson and the
database.

**Why full stack rather than `@WebMvcTest`:** `@WebMvcTest` starts only the web layer and needs
the service replaced by a mock. For a read-only endpoint with no branching, the full path to a
real database is more convincing and needs no mocking library. When the error paths arrive
(`400`/`404`), a `@WebMvcTest` with a mocked service may become the better fit. For the `404` of
`GET /inventory/{skuId}` we stayed full stack: "missing" just means "no row", which is easy to set
up for real, and it checks the whole path from the empty query to the plain-text response. The
`POST` tests stay full stack too: several of its `400`s come from Spring and Jackson *before* the
controller runs (unreadable JSON, wrong content type, `@Valid`), and one comes from the database's
answer (overflow), so a mocked service would skip exactly the parts being tested.

**Kotlin:** `@Autowired constructor` is explained in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

**Spring: context caching.** This class uses a different set of annotations from
`InventoryApplicationTests`, so Spring caches a separate context for it, with its own Postgres
container (see [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).

### A clean table before every test

```kotlin
/** Starts every test from an empty table, since all tests in this context share one database. */
@BeforeEach
fun clearInventory() {
    jdbcClient.sql("DELETE FROM inventory").update()
}
```

**Spring / JUnit: `@BeforeEach`.** JUnit calls this before each `@Test` method.

**Why explicit cleanup instead of `@Transactional` rollback** (which `InventoryRepositoryTest`
uses): rollback only covers work done on the test's own thread. MockMvc happens to run on that
thread, but tests that write from many threads at once can't rely on it (see
[InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md)). Explicit cleanup keeps every
full-context test on the same pattern.
Cleaning up *before* each test instead of after means a test that crashes halfway can't break
the next one.

The `insert` and `quantityOf` helpers are the same as in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

### Helpers for POST

```kotlin
private fun postInventory(
    skuId: String,
    body: String,
    mediaType: MediaType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON,
): ResultActionsDsl =
    mockMvc.post("/inventory/$skuId") {
        contentType = mediaType
        content = body
    }

private fun ResultActionsDsl.andExpectBadRequest(message: String) = andExpect {
    status { isBadRequest() }
    content {
        contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        string(message)
    }
}
```

**Kotlin: default arguments.** `mediaType: MediaType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON` gives the
parameter a default, so most calls are `postInventory("widget", body)` and only the content-type
test passes a third argument. Java has no default arguments; you'd write an overload
`postInventory(skuId, body)` that calls the three-argument one.

**Kotlin: the request-building lambda.** `mockMvc.post(url) { ... }` is another extension
function, like `get`. Its lambda has a request builder as its receiver, so `contentType = ...`
and `content = ...` set that builder's properties. The body is sent exactly as written. Nothing
parses it on the way out, which is how the tests can send broken JSON.

**Kotlin: writing your own extension function.** `ResultActionsDsl.andExpectBadRequest` is
declared here, in the test class, and it's `private`, so it exists only inside this class. It lets
every `400` test say `postInventory(...).andExpectBadRequest("...")` in one line. Inside it,
`andExpect { ... }` is called on `this`, the `ResultActionsDsl` it was called on. The return type
is inferred from `andExpect`, which returns the same `ResultActionsDsl`, so calls can chain.

**Why `null` and not an exception:** the same reasoning as `findBySkuId`. The repository reports
what happened ("no row was changed") and the service decides that it means a `400`.

### Case-sensitive add

```kotlin
// Why: SKU ids are an exact, case-sensitive match (README "Contract gaps" decision, 2026-09-28).
/** Adding to `WIDGET` creates a new SKU; it does not touch `widget`. */
@Test
fun `addStock treats SKU ids case-sensitively`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    assertEquals(InventoryItem("WIDGET", 2), inventoryRepository.addStock("WIDGET", 2))
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** the upsert's conflict check (`ON CONFLICT (sku_id)`) uses the primary key, which
compares `TEXT` exactly. So `WIDGET` doesn't conflict with `widget` and gets its own row.

### The database backstop

```kotlin
@Test
fun `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative`() {
    insert("widget", 1)

    assertFailsWith<DataIntegrityViolationException> {
        jdbcClient.sql("UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 2 WHERE sku_id = ?")
            .param("widget")
            .update()
    }
}
```

**Why this bypasses the repository:** the point is to show what happens if application code
is wrong. The `UPDATE` deliberately has no `quantity >= ?` guard, so the only thing stopping it
is the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint from
[V1__create_inventory.sql](../../main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).

**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { ... }`.** It runs the lambda and passes only if the lambda throws
a `T`. It returns the exception if you want to inspect it. `T` is a reified type parameter (see
[InventoryApplication.kt](../../main/InventoryApplication.kt.md)), which is how the function can
check the exception type at runtime. JUnit's version is `assertThrows(X.class, () -> ...)`.

**Spring:** Postgres answers with SQLSTATE `23514` (check violation). Spring's exception
translation maps it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, a database-independent exception, so
the test doesn't depend on Postgres error codes.

The failed statement aborts the test's transaction in Postgres, and the rollback at the end of
the test discards everything anyway.

content.text: okay lets begin with step 1

Step 1 is `PurchaseResult.kt`. It's a small file, but it uses three Kotlin ideas you haven't met yet in this project.

### Concept 1: `sealed interface`

A normal interface can be implemented by anyone, anywhere. A **sealed** interface can only be implemented by types declared in the same package and module, in practice the same file. So the compiler knows the complete list of implementations.

That matters because of `when`. In step 4 you'll write `when (result) { … }`. If the compiler knows there are exactly three cases and you handle all three, it needs no `else`. If someone adds a fourth case later, every `when` that doesn't handle it stops compiling. The compiler finds the places you forgot, so you don't have to.

**Java equivalent:** Java 17's `sealed interface PurchaseResult permits Purchased, SkuNotFound, InsufficientStock`, used with pattern-matching `switch`. Kotlin doesn't need the `permits` list, because the compiler works it out from what's declared.

### Concept 2: nested declarations

In Kotlin you can declare classes and objects **inside** the body of an interface. They are then referred to through the outer name: `PurchaseResult.Purchased`, which is what the tests use. Each nested case still has to say it implements the interface, using the same `: SomeType` syntax you already use for `: RuntimeException(...)` in your exceptions.

### Concept 3: `data class` vs `data object`

- A case that **carries data** is a `data class` with a `val` in its constructor, like `InventoryItem`. `Purchased` carries the `InventoryItem` with the remaining stock.
- A case that **carries nothing** doesn't need a new instance each time. An `object` is a singleton: exactly one instance, created by Kotlin. A `data object` adds a readable `toString()` (it prints `SkuNotFound` instead of `PurchaseResult$SkuNotFound@1a2b3c`) and a sensible `equals`. Your test failure messages will read better because of it.

**Java equivalent of an object:** a class with a private constructor and a `static final INSTANCE` field. Kotlin writes that as one keyword.

### A parallel example, from a different domain

```kotlin
sealed interface PaymentResult {
    data class Approved(val receiptId: String) : PaymentResult
    data object Declined : PaymentResult
    data object CardExpired : PaymentResult
}
```

Usage: `PaymentResult.Approved("r-123")` and `PaymentResult.Declined`. There's no `()` after an object, because you don't construct it.

### Your file needs

1. The `// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md` header line, then the package line.
2. KDoc on the interface: what it represents and where it sits in the flow (returned by the repository, translated by the service).
3. KDoc on **each** of the three cases. They're non-private declarations, so the standard applies to them too. One line each is enough.
4. A `// Why:` comment on the decision: a sealed type instead of `InventoryItem?`, and what was rejected.

When you've written it, say the word. I'll review it, and then we'll start on the CTE.

content.text:
Step 2 is the heart of the feature: `removeStock`. There are two parts, the SQL and then the row mapping.

### Try it by hand first (recommended)

Your Compose database isn't running right now. Start it and open `psql`:
```
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec postgres psql -U inventory
```
The `inventory` table only exists once Flyway has run, which happens at app startup. Inside `psql`, the quickest route is a scratch copy that disappears when you quit:
```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE inventory (sku_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0));
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES ('widget', 5), ('sold-out', 0);
```
In `psql`, you write literal values where your Kotlin will have `:skuId` and `:quantity`.

### Concept 1: the conditional `UPDATE` (you've seen its shape already)

It's in the README decision record: `UPDATE … SET quantity = quantity - N WHERE sku_id = … AND quantity >= N RETURNING sku_id, quantity`. On its own, it returns **one row** (purchased) or **zero rows**, and zero rows is ambiguous: missing SKU, or not enough stock? That ambiguity is why you need the CTE.

### Concept 2: a data-modifying CTE

`WITH <name> AS ( <statement> ) SELECT …` gives a sub-statement a name, and the main `SELECT` can then read `<name>` like a table. In Postgres, the statement inside the `WITH` can be an `UPDATE … RETURNING`. Whatever it `RETURNING`s is what `<name>` contains: one row or none.

Try this in `psql`: `WITH updated AS (…your UPDATE…) SELECT * FROM updated;`. Try it for widget with 2, sold-out with 1, and a missing SKU. You'll see the problem: the failure cases give **zero rows**, so you've lost the information again.

### Concept 3: make the outer `SELECT` always return exactly one row

A `SELECT` with **no `FROM`** (for example `SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS b;`) always returns exactly one row. Fill its columns with subqueries:
- A **scalar subquery**, `(SELECT … FROM updated)` in a column slot, gives that single value, or `NULL` when the subquery found no rows.
- **`EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = …)`** gives `true` or `false`.

So you end up with one row and two columns: "remaining quantity, or `NULL`" and "does the SKU exist". Run all three cases in `psql` and write down the pair you get for each. That table of three pairs is the spec for your mapping code.

A subtlety to ask me about later, because it's good interview material: the `EXISTS` reads the table *as it was when the statement started*, not after the update. Think about why that's harmless here.

### Part 2: mapping the row in Kotlin

- It's the same `jdbcClient.sql(…).param(…).query { rs, _ -> … }` chain you already know. Named parameters can appear more than once in the SQL (`:quantity` is used twice) and are still bound once.
- The query always returns exactly one row. Look at what `JdbcClient` offers besides `.list().singleOrNull()` when you *know* there's exactly one row.
- Inside the lambda, turn the two columns into one of the three `PurchaseResult` cases, using your table of three pairs.
- ⚠️ One of the columns can be SQL `NULL`. Decide deliberately how you read it into Kotlin, so that `NULL` ("nothing bought") can't be mistaken for `0` ("bought the last unit"). The last-unit test and the sold-out test exist to catch exactly that mix-up.

Docs: KDoc on `removeStock` (the three outcomes, and that `quantity` must be at least 1, like `addStock`), plus `// Why:` for "one statement, not update-then-select".

Start with the SQL in `psql`, and show me the three result pairs, or ask for a hint if you get stuck.

Close, but it's neither. The return type is **`PurchaseResult`**, non-null:

```kotlin
fun removeStock(skuId: String, quantity: Int): PurchaseResult
```

Here's the reasoning.

- **Why not `InventoryItem`:** an `InventoryItem` can only describe success. If the function promised an `InventoryItem`, what would it return when the SKU is missing? It would have to throw, and that's the "repository makes HTTP decisions" option you rejected in your `// Why:`.
- **Why not `InventoryItem?`:** that's `addStock`'s approach. `null` covers one failure, but there are two, and `null` can't say which.
- **Why `PurchaseResult`:** the sealed interface **is** the answer to "what does this function return". All three outcomes are `PurchaseResult`s. The `InventoryItem` is still there, one level down, inside the success case: `PurchaseResult.Purchased(item)`.
- **Why no `?`:** every outcome, including both failures, now has its own case. `null` would mean a fourth outcome, "no answer at all", which can't happen. The query always returns exactly one row.

This also changes what your `query { rs, _ -> … }` lambda builds. In `addStock`, the lambda built an `InventoryItem`. In `removeStock`, it builds a `PurchaseResult`: one of `PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem(...))`, `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` or `PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock`, chosen from the two columns.

In Java terms: the declared type is the interface, and each `return` hands back one of its implementations. It's like declaring `List` and returning an `ArrayList`.

**The CTE name labels a table, not a value.** Whatever you name it holds the rows the `UPDATE` changed: one row if the purchase went through, zero rows if it didn't. What are the ?

They're **positional parameter placeholders**, JDBC's plain-Java way of marking "a value goes here". Each `?` is filled by position: the first `.param(...)` fills the first `?`, the second fills the second, and so on. You've seen them in the test helpers: `VALUES (?, ?)` followed by `.params(skuId, quantity)`.

In that README snippet, they mean:

| `?` | Holds | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1st: `quantity - ?` | the quantity being bought | how much to subtract |
| 2nd: `sku_id = ?` | the SKU id | which row |
| 3rd: `quantity >= ?` | the quantity being bought (again) | only if there's enough |

The purchase quantity appears **twice**. With positional `?`, you'd have to pass it twice, in the right order, which is easy to get wrong.

**In your Kotlin, use named parameters instead**, as you did in `addStock`: `:quantity` and `:skuId`. A name can appear several times in the SQL, and one `.param("quantity", quantity)` fills every occurrence. Order no longer matters. So the `UPDATE` inside your CTE becomes the README's statement with `?` swapped for `:quantity`, `:skuId`, `:quantity`, and the `EXISTS` subquery reuses `:skuId` too.

**In `psql`, write the actual values**, because there's nothing there to bind parameters. For example `quantity - 2`, `sku_id = 'widget'` and `quantity >= 2`. Note the single quotes around text values in SQL.

Both kinds of placeholder exist for the same reason you noted in your `findBySkuId` comment: the value is sent separately from the SQL text, so it can never be read as SQL. That's the SQL-injection protection.
